name: Flint Grey
lede: Flint Grey is a light, grayish yellowish brown from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, placed at the very start of their plate sequence with a first-recorded date of 1000.

sections.title: Plate 14, dated to the year 1000
sections.body: Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary lists Flint Grey on plate 14, swatch A1, with a first-recorded date of 1000, far earlier than most of their entries and without a cited source for that date [1]. Two close neighbors on a nearby plate, Flesh Blonde and Touquet, are instead dated to the 1920s, in the book's usual range [1]. Our own classification places the hue in the ISCC-NBS region called light grayish yellowish brown, Munsell notation 1.5Y 6.0/2.0 [2]. The nearest named colors on file are [[grey-beige]], [[light-drab]], [[light-greyish-olive]] and [[pearl-beige]], at 3.6, 3.7, 4.6 and 5 ΔE [2]. Despite its name, Flint Grey reads as a warm, muted tan rather than a true gray, [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Flint Grey covers at least five percent of the canvas in 4,533 of them, about 19.1 percent overall, the single most common color, as photographed [3]. It is strongest in East Asian paintings, appearing in 48.1 percent of Japanese and 46.6 percent of Chinese works, well above the archive average [3]. Shen Zhou carries it in 11 of his 12 archived paintings, and its leading companion word is Taupe [3]. These counts read photographs of varnished paintings, not pigments [3].

origin.named_after: undocumented; a dictionary-of-color name, not a documented place or substance, despite sharing a word with the mineral flint
origin.first_recorded: dated to 1000 in Maerz and Paul (1930), without a cited source for that date
